name: Tryptophan
short: Occasional tremor, nausea and dizziness, mainly at higher doses; rare serotonin syndrome with serotonergic medicines. A 1989 eosinophilia-myalgia outbreak was linked to contaminated supplements.
text: A review of supplemental tryptophan reported occasional side effects, seen mainly at higher doses (70-200 mg/kg in the cited review), including tremor, nausea and dizziness, along with drowsiness; it noted that the evidence base is small and largely anecdotal. The same review states that in rare cases serotonin syndrome (with symptoms including delirium, myoclonus, hyperthermia and coma) occurs when tryptophan is combined with medicines that enhance serotonin function, such as antidepressants. In 1989 an epidemic of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome, marked by muscle pain and a high eosinophil count and followed in many patients by chronic skin lesions, progressive neuropathy and myopathy, was associated with L-tryptophan supplements; the later review states that the cause was shown to be a contaminant in certain production batches rather than tryptophan itself. In a randomised crossover study in 17 healthy women, up to 5.0 g/d for 21 days did not affect general blood and urine biomarkers or mood measures.
